headline: 2026 is the new 2016: the internet replays a decade

sources.title: It's 2016 Again, TikTok Users Have Declared, Using Decade-Old Songs And Filters (Forbes)
Fetty Wap, Zara Larsson & More: How 2016 Nostalgia Is Impacting Charts (Billboard)
'2026 Is the New 2016': Inside the Nostalgia Wave Taking Over Your Feed (Central Jersey)
Zara Larsson on her viral 'Lush Life' dance trend (video, Jennifer Hudson Show)

chunks.text: Open a video app this year, and you may think your phone traveled back in time. Ten years have {{gone by}}, but millions of people are {{looking back}} at 2016 with warm smiles. In January, new videos under the [[hashtag]] 2016 {{blew up}}, growing by more than 450 percent, and [[searches]] for 2016 songs [[jumped]] 290 percent. The internet has decided that 2026 is the new 2016.

verbs.why: Years go by, summers go by, and sometimes a whole childhood goes by before you notice it. A full ten years have gone by since 2016, and this year the internet decided to notice.
People look back on their childhood, look back with regret, or just look back at old photos for fun. Here millions of fans look back at 2016 with nothing but warm smiles.
A photo can blow up online overnight, a rumor can blow up in a group chat, and a small joke can blow up into a trend. Here the 2016 hashtag blew up in January, growing by more than 450 percent.

chunks.text: The [[nostalgia]] is easy to see on the street. Teens {{dress up}} in [[chokers]], [[skinny jeans]], and [[wired headphones]], filming videos in the flat, bright style of old phones. Photo apps {{brought back}} [[beloved]] tricks like the famous dog-ears [[filter]], and the [[mannequin challenge]], where whole rooms freeze like [[statues]], {{came back}} [[from the dead]]. For one video, at least, it is 2016 again.

verbs.correct: To wear special or fancy clothes
verbs.wrong: To buy clothes you do not need
verbs.why: People dress up for parties, dress up for costume contests, and sometimes just dress up for no reason at all. This year teens dress up in chokers and skinny jeans to enjoy the whole look of 2016 all over again.

verbs.correct: To return something from the past
verbs.why: Stores bring back old recipes, radio stations bring back forgotten songs, and apps now bring back old photo filters too. Here photo apps brought back the famous dog-ears filter that everyone used a decade ago.
Old trends come back, forgotten songs come back, and sometimes a whole decade comes back all at once. Here the mannequin challenge has come back, with whole rooms freezing like statues again.

chunks.text: The clearest sign is the music. Thanks to a viral dance, Swedish singer Zara Larsson's 2016 hit Lush Life re-entered the British [[charts]] at number eight and returned to the American list, a full [[decade]] after its [[release]]. Fans say the bright, simple pop of that year still {{holds up}} today, and old songs by other 2016 [[stars]] are climbing again too. What was once just a [[playlist]] has {{turned into}} a giant online party.

verbs.correct: To stay good as time passes
verbs.why: A good joke can hold up for years, and an old song can hold up even better. Fans say Zara Larsson's 2016 hit still holds up today, a full decade after its release.
A hobby can turn into a career, and a small argument can turn into a big fight. Here a private playlist of old songs turned into a giant online party that everyone wanted to join.

chunks.text: Why 2016? Psychologists point to [[timing]]. Many fans call it the last year before the world got complicated, and the trend is strongest among tired people who wish life would {{slow down}} a little. There is also a younger crowd: today's teenagers were small children in 2016, so they {{missed out on}} the fun the first time. Experts add one [[warning]] about the nostalgia [[cycle]]: it is {{speeding up}}, with each [[revival]] arriving sooner than the last. And the [[rerun]] always looks better than the [[original]], because the videos {{leave out}} the bad days. That year had them too.

verbs.correct: To move at a calmer speed
verbs.why: Traffic slows down before a red light, a runner slows down near the finish line, and life slows down once summer ends. Many tired fans just wish life would slow down a little, the way it feels in old memories.

verbs.correct: To lose the chance to enjoy something
verbs.why: Shoppers miss out on a sale, latecomers miss out on the best seats, and quiet kids sometimes miss out on the fun. Today's teenagers missed out on 2016 the first time around, since they were only small children then.

A heartbeat can speed up during a scary movie, and traffic can speed up once the road opens. Experts say the nostalgia cycle itself is speeding up, with each new trend arriving sooner than the one before it.

A story can leave out the hard parts, a recipe can leave out one key ingredient, and a memory can leave out the bad days entirely. These 2016 videos leave out the difficult moments, so the whole year looks better than it really was.

mainIdea.s: Ten years later, the internet is celebrating 2016 with old fashion, filters, and music, and a decade-old pop song is back on the charts. Experts say people miss a simpler time.
mainIdea.why: The 2016 hashtag blew up, chokers and old filters returned, and Lush Life re-entered the British top ten.

mainIdea.s: A Swedish singer released a brand new album this month that copies the sound of 2016. Helped by one viral dance, it instantly reached number eight on the British charts.
mainIdea.why: Close, but Lush Life is not new. Her actual 2016 song re-entered the charts a full decade after its release.

mainIdea.s: Video apps announced that the oldest filters and dances will be deleted this year because teenagers find them embarrassing. Fans are now fighting to save their favorites.
mainIdea.why: It is the opposite. Apps brought back old filters, and fans are happily replaying the whole year.
